prime.problem: Seven courses have handed you dozens of levers: batching, FP8, speculative decoding, better kernels, TP/PP layouts, disaggregation, routing, autoscaling, training choices. Without one formula they all feed, you can't rank them, see which ones compete, or explain a price to a customer.
prime.fits: The capstone map of the whole Fast LLM inference series. It reuses course 2's step formula and course 5–6's engine and layout levers, and previews this course's two halves: what training costs and hands over, and what a served token costs.
expect: $/M = price per GPU-hour ÷ (tokens per second × 3600 × busy share)
which layer of the stack moves which term
the ranked levers and their multipliers
why a smaller, over-trained model is cheaper forever
prime.goal: Place any optimization from the series on one term of the $/M formula, estimate its multiplier, and explain why the levers don't simply multiply.

attend: Every lever changes one of three things. What are they, and which layer of the stack owns each?
Why is batching the biggest lever, and what does the user pay for it?
Why does FP8 help least exactly where batching helps most?
Why does the serving bill overtake the training bill after about 3D served tokens?
Market prices already sit below our BF16 ceiling. What does that tell you about how to read the table?

must: A token's price = the hour's price ÷ tokens made in that hour → every optimization changes the hour's price (GPU, spot), tokens per step (batch, bytes, speculation, kernels, layout) or the busy share (autoscaling, routing, reliability) → rank levers as multipliers on one line

Decode reads the weights once per step for the whole batch → batching B = 1 → 238 makes tokens 48.6× cheaper but each user 4.9× slower → the latency you promise sets the batch, and the batch sets the price

Levers compete for the same slack → speculation fills idle compute at small batch and fades as the batch grows; FP8 weights halve the weight read, which dominates only at small batch → multipliers don't stack cleanly, so re-run the formula at your operating point

Training is paid once (6ND) and serving 2N per token forever → after ~3D served tokens serving costs more → a smaller model trained longer (8B on 15T) is ~4.4× cheaper per served token than the Chinchilla-optimal size for the same training budget
elevated: Input tokens go through compute-bound prefill (~$0.018/M at peak) and output tokens through bandwidth-bound decode ($0.111/M at best) → prices are split in and out, and levers that cut prefill (prefix routing, caching) act on the cheap side unless prompts are long
reference: the full ranked-lever table and its sources
the training table's per-card rules of thumb
the source quirks list (16/20/10/15 bytes, 30.1% misprint, 545% margin)

compress.prompt: Draw the whole course (and series) as one causal map: the $/M formula in the middle, the six stack layers around it with an arrow from each to the term it moves, and the training half feeding in from the side through model size. Label the three biggest multipliers.
checklist: GPU → p and the speed limit; kernels and engine → T_step and B; cluster layout → fit and T_step; router/autoscaler → u
training choices → model size N → bytes per step for every served token
biggest: batching (~49×), FP8 weights + KV at the largest batch (~2.1×), autoscaling vs peak provisioning (~1.9×)
levers compete for the same slack, so they don't simply multiply

retrieve.q: Explain why a serving business is "a choice of operating point" rather than a price list.
answer: the same GPU-hour gives $5.40 or $0.111 per M depending on the batch
the batch also sets each user's speed (205 vs 42 tok/s)
so the latency promise picks the batch, and the batch picks the price

retrieve.q: Walk through the filled-in formula at B = 238, and then at 25% utilization.
answer: at u = 0.25, divide by 0.25: $0.44 per M

retrieve.q: You have one quarter to cut $/M for an 8B service already running at B = 64. Rank three levers from the table and say what each costs you.
answer: FP8 weights and KV: fits a bigger batch; needs a quality check (evals, canary)
autoscale with a warm floor: raises u (36% → 68% on the example day); risks cold starts at the edges
better kernels: 70% → 100% of the ceiling is $0.245 → $0.172; costs engineering (or an AI-kernel loop with anti-cheat checks)
speculative decoding helps latency more than cost at this batch

retrieve.q: Use the training table to size Llama-3.1-8B's run: compute, memory, and how it's fitted onto GPUs.
answer: 6ND = 7.2e23 FLOPs → 0.51M H100-hours at 40% MFU, ~$2.0M
128.5 GB state + 36.5 GB activations at 8k (selective) = 165 GB, 2.1 H100s
ZeRO-3 on 8 GPUs: 16.1 GB of state per GPU at 1.5× communication

compare.q: The series map lays out the stack layer by layer; this card lays out the same layers by the term of the $/M formula they move. What does the cost view reveal that the stack view hides?
answer: the stack view says where a technique lives; the cost view says how much it's worth
it shows the levers compete (speculation vs batching, FP8 vs batching) instead of stacking
and it puts the router and autoscaler, which change no kernel, on equal footing through u

compare.q: Course 2's step formula ends in milliseconds; this card ends in dollars. Which two terms are added between them, and which levers act only through those?
answer: the hour's price p and the busy share u
p: choice of GPU, provider, spot vs on-demand
u: autoscaling, routing (fewer repeated prefills), reliability (fewer dropped hours)

compare.q: The overview's last lever is "train a smaller model longer". Which quantity links the training half of the course to the serving half, and how does it enter each formula?
answer: model size N (and its bytes W)
training: C = 6ND sets the one-time bill
serving: W/BW and 2BN/C set every step's time, so N enters every token's price

predict.q: FP8 weights only (KV cache stays BF16) on the 8B. Commit before reading on: is the price cut bigger at B = 1 or at the largest batch that fits, and roughly how big is each?
predict.answer: Bigger at B = 1: about 1.97× ($5.40 → $2.75), because the step is almost all weight reading. At the largest batch it's only 1.13× ($0.111 → $0.099): KV reads dominate the step there, and the freed 8 GB fits only 268 sequences instead of 238. Adding FP8 KV too (536 sequences) makes it 2.1× at the largest batch.

apply.task: Price one realistic service with the formula. Llama-3.1-8B on H100s at $3.99, a promise of at least 100 tok/s per user, 2k context. (1) Which row of the batch table does the promise allow, and what is $/M at u = 1? (2) Traffic keeps the fleet 50% busy: new $/M? (3) Move to AWS spot at $2.60: new $/M? (4) Your kernels actually reach 85% of the ceiling (the step takes 9.92 ÷ 0.85 ms): new $/M at spot and u = 0.5? (5) Name the one lever from the overview table you'd pull next and why.
apply.done: (1) B = 64, 101 tok/s per user, $0.172/M. (2) $0.344/M. (3) $0.224/M. (4) 11.67 ms step, 5,483 tok/s, $0.263/M. (5) Any defended choice; e.g. autoscaling to raise u, since 50% idle costs more (2×) than every kernel or GPU-price lever here.
